rashi:a1.1: And their sanctity ceased: from the time of the census in the book of Numbers [Ḥumash HaPekudim] onward.
gershom:a1.1: Granted, according to Reish Lakish: who said they were sanctified and then ceased. As he said, the reason is that the firstborn were sanctified [again] upon their entry into Eretz Yisrael; evidently they had been sanctified in the wilderness and then ceased.
rashi:a2.1: His reason: from “And it shall be when He shall bring you,” and only then “and you shall set apart.”
gershom:a2.1: But according to Rabbi Yoḥanan: who said they did not cease, what is the reason?
gershom:a3.1: “I saw Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream”: therefore the matter is supported, that I explain the reason well. The verse states “they shall be”: in their state they shall be, meaning they were sanctified and did not cease.
rashi:a4.1: This mitzva: of the firstborn, on account of which you will enter the land; and that is why the Merciful One placed them next to each other.
gershom:a4.1: On account of which you will enter the land: in the merit of fulfilling it.
gershom:a5.1: And do you also reverse the objection: where it says “Reish Lakish raised an objection to Rabbi Yoḥanan”? And do you also reverse that of Rabbi Elazar, so that you say “I saw Reish Lakish in a dream”?
rashi:a6.1: And do you also reverse that of Rabbi Elazar: and say “I saw Reish Lakish in a dream,” and he explains Reish Lakish’s statement? But Rabbi Elazar was Rabbi Yoḥanan’s student!
rashi:a6.2: He said to him: this “they were not sanctified” that Rabbi Yoḥanan says means that they did not need to be consecrated. If one wishes to sacrifice them, he need not consecrate them as one does other non-sacred animals, for they were sacred from the moment they were born. This is the same as above, that according to Rabbi Yoḥanan the firstborn were sanctified in the wilderness.
gershom:a6.1: He said to him: We do not reverse [those], for this is what it teaches us in our version: what is the “they were not sanctified” that Rabbi Yoḥanan said? The firstborn in the wilderness did not need to be sanctified, since they had been sanctified in Egypt and the sanctity never ceased.
rashi:a7.1: In the language of his teacher: even though both explanations come to the same thing, he nevertheless told it to him in the language in which he had learned it.
gershom:a7.1: If so, that is our version: yes, indeed. But the reason we reversed it is that a person must say [what he learned] in the language of his teacher.
rashi:a8.1: Kontrokos: the name of an officer.
rashi:a8.2: In the individual count of the Levites: for Gershon it is written (Numbers 3:22) seven thousand five hundred, and for Kehat it is written (3:28) eight thousand six hundred, which makes sixteen thousand one hundred; and for Merari it is written (3:34) six thousand two hundred, which makes twenty-two thousand three hundred. And in their collective count it is written (3:39): “All the males from a month old and upward, twenty-two thousand.”
gershom:a8.1: In the individual count of the Levites: where it counts the sons of Gershon, the sons of Kehat and the sons of Merari. When you combine their count, you find 22,300.
gershom:a9.1: And in the collective count: where it counts them together, they are only 22,000.
gershom:a10.1: It is enough for a Levite firstborn to abrogate his own sanctity.
rashi:a10.1: Half a shekel, of the shekel of the Sanctuary: per head, for 603,550, which makes 201 talents and eleven maneh. A talent is sixty maneh, and a maneh is a hundred dinars, which are twenty-five sela, and the Torah’s shekel is a sela. Multiply sixty by twenty-five and you find 1,500 sela in a talent, which are 3,000 half-shekels. So for 3,000 Israelites you find a talent of silver; for 300,000, a hundred talents; for 600,000, two hundred talents. For [the remaining] 3,000, 1,500 sela; for 500 men, 250 sela; and for 50 men, 25 sela: that makes 1,775 sela. Combine the sela and make maneh of them, four maneh for every hundred sela: so for 1,000 sela, forty maneh, and for 500 sela, twenty maneh, which makes a talent. There remain 275 sela, which are eleven maneh.
gershom:a11.1: In the collection of the silver: when he collected half a shekel from each one, and when you combine them their count comes to 201 talents and eleven maneh. How? The maneh is twenty-five shekels, which is a hundred dinars, and a hundred half-shekels are two maneh. It follows that 3,000 half-shekels are sixty maneh, for that is the talent of the Sanctuary, sixty maneh, as we derive below from the verses, from “a hundred talents” and from “seventy talents.” From this you can understand: as 3,000 make one talent, so 300,000 make a hundred talents and 600,000 two hundred talents. That is why it says 201 talents. And 550 half-shekels are eleven maneh. But in the giving of the silver, where he gave an accounting to Israel, you find only a hundred talents.
rashi:a11.1: And he did not return a complete half: for of the half he should have paid a hundred and a half talents and five and a half maneh, and he gave only a hundred talents, as it is written, “a hundred talents.” And even though it is written, “And of the 1,775 [shekels] he made hooks for the pillars” (Exodus 38:28), which shows that he returned more than half, the officer did not mention that verse, since he intended to provoke him with words.
tosafot:a11.1: Kuveyustus: elsewhere, in Ḥullin (91b), Rashi explained it as a kidnapper; but that meaning does not fit here, where the subject is collecting silver. [Rashi explains it the same way] in the chapter HaMokher Peirot (Bava Batra 92b), with regard to slaves, and ordinary slaves are not kidnappers. Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained it as a dice player. And as for what is said in Bereshit Rabba on “Let me go, for the dawn has broken” (Genesis 32:27), “Are you a thief or a kuveyustus, that you are afraid of the dawn?”: it is the way of a dice player to hide himself, because he loses money at the game and becomes indebted on credit.
tosafot:a11.2: And he did not return a complete half: the officer did not mention to him the verse “And of the 1,775 [shekels] he made hooks for the pillars,” since he intended to provoke him.
gershom:a13.1: He intended to disparage him: “and he did not return a complete half,” for half of the one talent and eleven maneh was still lacking.
rashi:a12.1: Was double: a talent held 120 maneh, so those hundred talents were two hundred talents, and the one talent and eleven maneh were the 1,775 [shekels] of which he made hooks for the pillars.
gershom:a14.1: And a maneh of the Sanctuary was double: of two hundred dinars. So two hundred talents are a hundred talents, and the talent and eleven maneh, since they did not amount to a doubled Sanctuary talent, the verse did not count [as a talent]. It said only, “And the hundred talents of silver were,” and the talent and eleven maneh are the full 1,775 shekels, as it is written, “And of the 1,775…”
rashi:a13.1: Another verse is written: in which “for casting” is not written, and it counts the whole sum.
gershom:a15.1: What posed a difficulty: for Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai? What forced him to answer that the [Sanctuary] maneh was double? Let him tell him: those hundred talents of which the verse speaks were for casting, and the rest was placed in the treasury.
gershom:a16.1: He could not answer him that way, because another verse is written, “And the silver of those that were numbered of the congregation was a hundred talents,” and “for casting” is not written there. That is why he told him it was double.
tosafot:a14.1: From where does he derive this: that is, [the Gemara asks] he should have some source from which to infer this matter, other than this difficulty.
gershom:a17.1: And from where does he derive that it was double?
rashi:a15.1: If we say from it: from this verse itself. For since there are 1,775, that comes to seventy-one maneh. And even if he returned only what is written, still the verse should have counted these as a talent and eleven maneh; it did not count them so, but itemized [befrutrot], in their details, and did not make a total of them to reckon them as a talent. Learn from it that [the Sanctuary maneh] was double.
tosafot:a15.1: Here there are seventy-one maneh: and the verse counted them only in small coins.
gershom:a18.1: If we say from it: from that verse, “And the silver of those that were numbered of the congregation was a hundred talents and 1,775 shekels.” For here there are seventy-one maneh, since twenty-five shekels are a maneh and 1,775 shekels are seventy-one maneh. [The printed text is garbled at this point, and the editor proposes a correction.] The verse did not count them as a talent, even though there is more here than a simple talent of sixty [maneh], [plus] eleven maneh. It did not count them as a talent but itemized; “itemized” [befrutrot] means details, that is, it counted them in shekels, which are details. Evidently it counted them itemized because they did not contain the measure of a doubled [talent].
tosafot:a16.1: And a maneh of the Sanctuary was double: but common shekels and Sanctuary shekels were equal. And if you ask: in any case, let the verse count them in maneh and say thirty-five and a half maneh; and likewise below, where it says “here there are ninety-six maneh,” it should have counted in maneh and said forty-eight maneh, and the maneh would be a more complete unit. One can answer that the weight of a maneh did not yet exist in Moses’ days, and nowhere does a verse in the Torah write “maneh.” Know that this is so: in the first chapter of Ketubot (10b), regarding a widow, we say she is called almana on account of the maneh, since the Rabbis would in the future institute a ketuba of a maneh for her. Does the verse write [a name] for the future? And why do we not infer [from it] that a widow’s ketuba is by Torah law? Rather, it must be because there was no maneh in Moses’ days.
rashi:a15.2: In fact one can still ask why he did not return two hundred talents. And as for what you said, that if it was not double, why did the verse not count them in talents: that is no reason, for general sums that reached a hundred it counts in totals, and details, such as one talent, it does not count in talents. Therefore it counted them itemized.
gershom:a19.1: But perhaps: we still do not learn from here that the maneh was double. The reason it did not count these 1,775 as a talent is that it counts general sums in talents and does not count details in talents; that is, a hundred talents, since a hundred is a general sum, it counts in talents, but one talent, which is a detail, it does not count in talents. So in fact it was not double, and the reason it did not count it as a talent is that it does not count details in talents.
rashi:a18.1: And 2,400 shekels: two thousand are eighty maneh, at four maneh for every hundred, and four hundred are sixteen maneh, which makes ninety-six maneh; and it counted them only itemized. Yet this verse does count details in talents, for it writes “seventy talents.” Since it did not write “seventy-one talents and thirty-six maneh,” learn from it that [the maneh] was double, and until there are 120 maneh it is not a talent.
gershom:a20.1: For here there is no general sum of talents: it is not a hundred talents but seventy talents, which are details of talents. And here, beyond the seventy talents, there are ninety-six maneh, for 2,400 shekels are ninety-six maneh, and it counted them only itemized. If the Sanctuary talent were simple, it should have said seventy-one talents and thirty-six maneh. Rather, since it counted them itemized, in shekels, learn from it that the talents were double, and those shekels did not amount to a doubled talent.
rashi:a19.1: A large detail: seventy. It calls it a detail because it did not reach a hundred.
rashi:a19.2: A small detail: for example, one talent.
gershom:a21.1: But perhaps: in fact it was not double. The reason it counts these itemized, though they contain more than a simple talent, is that a large detail, such as seventy talents, or sixty, or fifty, or twenty, or ten, it counts in talents; but a small detail, one, less than ten, it does not count in talents but itemized. So in fact let us say it is not double.
rashi:a20.1: And the shekel is twenty gera: it is a verse in Ezekiel: “twenty shekels… shall be your maneh.” Evidently the maneh is twenty-five sela [i.e., the common maneh, one of the verse’s parts].
tosafot:a20.1: And the shekel is twenty gera: that is, ma’a, as the Targum renders it, “twenty ma’a to the sela.” And this is puzzling, for it is said that a sela is four dinars and that six silver ma’a are a dinar; evidently there are twenty-four ma’a in a sela. Rabbeinu Tam explained that they added to the weight twice. In Ezekiel’s days, when the shekel was twenty gera, they added a sixth to the Sanctuary maneh, which at first held fifty sela, and made the Sanctuary maneh sixty; but to the shekel they added nothing. Then in the days of the Sages they again added a sixth to the shekel, besides the earlier addition: it had been twenty [ma’a] and they made it twenty-four. So according to Rabbeinu Tam, when the addition was made in Ezekiel’s days the Sanctuary maneh became more than double the common one, since the common maneh is always twenty-five sela and they made the Sanctuary one sixty sela. And in the days of the Sages, when they added to the sela, the Sanctuary maneh and the common maneh both grew automatically. And this is the meaning of Ezekiel’s verse, “And the shekel is twenty gera”: of those shekels that were originally twenty gera there are sixty in the present maneh, but of the present shekels, which became twenty-four [ma’a], it holds only fifty in the Sanctuary maneh and twenty-five in the common one.
tosafot:a20.2: In brief: Why does Ezekiel not simply say that sixty shekels are the maneh, and why does he divide them as twenty, twenty-five, and ten and five? Because these were the weights kept in the Temple: one weight of twenty shekels, with which they weighed a third of the Sanctuary maneh after the sixth was added; one of twenty-five, the size of a common maneh, [which Tosafot calls] a quarter of the Sanctuary maneh before it was increased; and one of fifteen. The three together make up a Sanctuary maneh. The Targum shows this too, rendering: “The sela is twenty ma’a; a third of a maneh is twenty sela; a maneh of silver is twenty-five sela; a quarter of a maneh is five and ten sela; all of them together are sixty, the great maneh, the Sanctuary maneh, shall it be for you.” On the other explanation, “a third of a maneh” and “a quarter of a maneh” do not fit as well; [the Targum] means the Sanctuary maneh after it was increased, and “a maneh of silver, twenty-five sela” means the common maneh before it was increased. And if you ask how we know that Ezekiel added anything at all, perhaps the Sanctuary maneh was sixty from the start: Moses’ hundred talents prove that originally the Sanctuary maneh was only [double] the common one. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b1.1: Rather, from here: “And the shekel is twenty gera; twenty shekels, twenty-five shekels, ten and five shekels shall be your maneh.” The verse’s sum is sixty shekels, and it says “shall be your maneh,” meaning that this is how the maneh shall be.
gershom:b2.1: A maneh? [Said] in astonishment: sixty shekels are 240 dinars, which is two maneh and a hundred dinars [so the text; 240 dinars is two maneh and forty dinars].
rashi:b1.1: But they are 240 dinars: rather, it was double, and a Sanctuary maneh held two hundred; and these forty more than that are what they added in Ezekiel’s days. They added a sixth to them, for forty is a sixth from the outside: in two hundred there are five times forty, and they brought another forty, a sixth from the outside, and added it. We do not say a sixth from the inside, that one divides [the original] into six and adds one of those parts to the weight.
gershom:b3.1: Rather, learn from it: since it says “shall be your maneh,” that a Sanctuary maneh was double; and these forty beyond two hundred are what they added to the measure, a sixth from the outside.
rashi:b3.1: In beit motva rabba: in the great study hall.
tosafot:b3.1: Ninety Nubian [luvim] donkeys: named for [Luv, as in] “Put and Lubim were your helpers” (Nahum 3:9) and “and the Lubim and the Kushim shall be at his steps” (Daniel 11:43). The “Luvian donkey” at the beginning of the chapter Bameh Behema (Shabbat 51b) the Arukh explains as an Egyptian donkey. And the Jerusalem Talmud reads: converts who come from Put and Luv, what is the law, must they wait three generations?
rashi:b4.1: That they slackened their hands, etc.: and therefore Amalek came upon them.
rashi:b4.2: The fathers look not back to their children because of feebleness of hands: from here [we learn the word means] that they slackened their hands from the Torah.
rashi:b5.1: In matters of nonsense: to commit harlotry with the daughters of Moab.
rashi:b6.1: Naked women encountered them: vatikrena implies that their bodies were encountering them.
gershom:b4.1: Naked women: were walking about and encountering the Israelites. That is vatikrena: they themselves, that is, their flesh, touched them, in order to inflame their desire.
rashi:b6.2: That they all became ones who experienced emissions: it is the language of mikreh [an occurrence, the term for an emission].
rashi:b7.1: Mishna. “Firstborn of a donkey,” “firstborn of a donkey,” twice: these are written in the Torah, once in [the passage] “Sanctify to Me every firstborn” (Exodus 13) and once in [the passage] “See, You say to me” (Exodus 33–34).
gershom:b5.1: “Firstborn of a donkey,” “firstborn of a donkey,” twice: once in the portion Bo el Paro and once in the portion Ki Tisa.
rashi:b7.2: The one that bears: the mother.
rashi:b7.3: And the one born is a donkey: that it resembles its mother.
rashi:b8.1: And what is their status with regard to consumption: those that do not resemble their mother.
gershom:b6.1: We learned there: in the other chapter.
rashi:b9.1: Gemara. Some of the characteristics: of its mother.
gershom:b7.1: From where are these matters derived: that it is exempt.
rashi:b10.1: But the firstborn of an ox, etc.: since it could have written “But an ox, a lamb and a goat,” for the passage is speaking of the firstborn, as written just before it, “everything that opens the womb,” etc., and yet it used “firstborn” with each of them, learn from it [that it is not sanctified] unless the firstborn is like its mother and does not resemble another kind.
rashi:b11.1: “But” makes a distinction: for every akh and rak [“but” and “only”] in the Torah comes to exclude.
tosafot:b11.1: The verse states “But,” making a distinction: this is puzzling. Our tanna, who does not have this exposition, from where does he derive that one with some of the characteristics is obligated? That is a mishna in chapter 2 (below, 16b), and it is not reasonable that it disagrees with [the mishna of] our chapter. Yet if they do not disagree, it is difficult that [the Gemara] cites [that mishna] together with a tanna who follows Rav Yehuda; and when it asks “From where are these matters derived?” it should have cited the verse of our mishna.
gershom:b8.1: “But” makes a distinction: if it has some characteristic by which it resembles its mother, it is obligated in the firstborn. And the same is true for the tanna of our mishna: even though it does not teach “and if it has some of the characteristics,” if it has some characteristics resembling its mother it is obligated, for so the Gemara asks below: “A dilemma was raised before them: a cow [that gave birth to]…”
rashi:b12.1: But doesn’t the tanna: of our mishna.
rashi:b12.2: Cite “firstborn,” “firstborn” with regard to a cow: for he derives that a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts is exempt from the firstborn from “firstborn,” “firstborn”: unless the one that bears is a donkey and the one born is a donkey; and he derives the cow too from the donkey. So how could Rav Yehuda set aside the verse of the mishna and adopt a different derivation?
tosafot:b12.1: But doesn’t the tanna cite “firstborn,” “firstborn” with regard to a cow: one cannot say that in any case the verse of the mishna is needed to exempt [the offspring] from the sanctity of a firstborn donkey, and the verse here to exempt it from the law of an ox. For “exempt from the firstborn,” taught in the mishna, implies that it exempts the cow entirely; this shows that “firstborn,” “firstborn” [and the verse of the ox] are derived from each other, as below. And if you ask: granted, from “firstborn,” “firstborn” we learn [the case of] a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts [so the text]; perhaps that applies only where it changed into something that has no inherent sanctity, but where, for example, a ewe gave birth to a goat of sorts, which has inherent sanctity, I would say it is sanctified. One can answer that it is entirely reasonable that we derive them from each other, sanctity of value from inherent sanctity, as is said shortly. But this is difficult, for it says that we do not derive even inherent sanctity from inherent sanctity, since for ox, lamb and goat a verse is needed for each one.
gershom:b9.1: But doesn’t the tanna cite “firstborn,” “firstborn”: this is asked against Rav Yehuda: why does he not derive it from “firstborn,” “firstborn,” from where the tanna of our mishna derives it? Had he found a baraita that derives it from “But the firstborn,” one could say that Rav Yehuda holds like it; but if he says it as his own statement, why does he not derive it from “firstborn,” “firstborn”? [The answer:] Yes, he found a baraita, and that is why it says “in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, as it is taught…”
rashi:b13.1: Rav Yehuda said it in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
gershom:b10.1: With regard to what do they disagree: why does the tanna derive it from “firstborn,” “firstborn,” and Rabbi Yosei from “But the firstborn”?
rashi:b15.1: The Merciful One revealed: with a donkey, which has sanctity of value, since it is sacred only for its value, in that one redeems it with a lamb, the Merciful One revealed that one that resembles [another kind] is exempt; and the same is true for the firstborn of a kosher animal, which has inherent sanctity.
gershom:b11.1: The tanna of our mishna holds: the Merciful One revealed it with regard to sanctity of value, which is the lighter, since a firstborn donkey can be redeemed, that it is not sanctified unless it is a donkey and its offspring a donkey.
gershom:b12.1: And the same is true: all the more so with inherent sanctity, the firstborn of a kosher animal, which cannot be redeemed, that it is not sanctified unless it is exactly in its likeness [like its mother].
gershom:b13.1: And Rabbi Yosei holds: the Merciful One revealed it with regard to inherent sanctity, and he derives sanctity of value from inherent sanctity by “just as we found.” For according to Rabbi Yosei one cannot say “and the same is true, all the more so,” since sanctity of value is the lighter; rather, [he derives it] by “just as we found.” And this is their dispute: one derives it by “the same is true” and the other by “just as we found.”
rashi:b18.1: Why were sacrificial portions stated, etc.: in this verse, “But the firstborn of an ox, or the firstborn of a lamb, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy; you shall sprinkle their blood… and make their fat burn,” [which teaches] that the sacrificial portions of all of them are offered.
gershom:b14.1: Why were sacrificial portions stated with a firstborn ox, sacrificial portions with a firstborn lamb, sacrificial portions with a firstborn goat: for it is written of all of them, “you shall sprinkle their blood on the altar and make their fat burn.” Why was it necessary to write it of all of them? Let it write the sacrificial portions with one, and derive the others from it.
rashi:b19.1: An ox: its libations are greater, half a hin, while a lamb and a goat have a quarter of a hin. A lamb: its tail is offered with the sacrificial portions, as is explained in Leviticus, which is not so for an ox and a goat.
gershom:b15.1: They are necessary: to write it with all of them. These cannot be derived from an ox, since an ox has more libations, half a hin for a bull. And had it written the sacrificial portions with a lamb, the others could not be derived from it, since a lamb has something that an ox and a goat lack: a lamb has more with its tail.
rashi:b23.1: A lamb and a goat: the Paschal offering comes from them, as it is written: “You shall take it from the sheep or from the goats” (Exodus 12:5).
gershom:b16.1: Both cannot be derived from one, but let one be derived from two: what about these, a lamb and a goat? It is reasonable that they have more with regard to sacrificial portions, since they have more with regard to the Paschal offering, which comes from them.
rashi:b24.1: An ox and a goat have an increase with regard to the community’s idol worship: a bull for a burnt offering and a goat for a sin offering.
gershom:b17.1: What about these: an ox and a goat, which have more with regard to communal idol worship, since a bull and a goat are brought, but not a lamb.
rashi:b25.1: An ox and a lamb have an element of increase with regard to the altar: when they are offered, more of them goes to the fires than of a goat: the ox in its libations, and the lamb in its tail.
gershom:b18.1: What about these: an ox and a lamb, which have an element of increase with regard to the altar: an ox in libations and a lamb in its tail. But a goat has no element of increase for the altar.
gershom:b19.1: Therefore it was necessary to write “their blood” and “their fat,” which refer to all of them.
rashi:b26.1: If so: that the verse comes only for this.
tosafot:b26.1: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: if so, let the verse write “But a firstborn ox, lamb and goat”: and the reason we expound from it “unless it is an ox and its firstborn an ox,” even though [the first “firstborn”] is needed for the teaching of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, is that, like the second and third “firstborn,” we should expound the first as well.
gershom:b20.1: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: who derives from this verse “unless it is an ox and its firstborn an ox.” If so, that it comes only for this, that the sacrificial portions of a firstborn ox, lamb [and goat are offered], let the verse write “But a firstborn ox, lamb and goat,” and that would suffice for the sacrificial portions. Why do I need “firstborn,” “firstborn”? …
gershom:b21.1: Learn from it: both are derived from it.
rashi:b29.1: And still I say: a firstborn donkey you shall redeem with a lamb and not with anything else, while other firstborn non-kosher animals are redeemed with anything, and they are in fact sanctified as firstborn.
